title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) review - this Switch 2 remake has reminded me Nintendo's masterpiece is still worth talking about for a reason
author: @eurogamer
content:
Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve.

I have a friend who first played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time back in the day, when the game was only just released and he was home from university for Christmas. This is objectively the best of all times to play any video game: not Christmas specifically, but dropped out of the regular world and faced with a few weeks filled with nothing pressing to do whatsoever. Years later, though, my friend told me that the magic of the game didn't just come down to the playing of it, but the way that the playing of it unfolded.

Here's what he meant. He'd play all day, curtains drawn, family ignored, working through dungeons and pelting across Hyrule Field on Epona. Then in the evening he'd call his girlfriend, who was back with her own family for Christmas. She always wanted to know what he'd got up to that day. And not in East Sussex; she wanted to know what he'd got up to in Hyrule.

So as he played he took regular breaks to tell someone else about what he had encountered, and what he had discovered, and what he had yet to overcome. It is my bright delight today to be able to tell you that, around thirty years later, having just revisited the game in Nintendo's new remake, Ocarina of Time is still worth telling people about. It's still an adventure so surprising, so satisfying, so moving that I need to talk about it.

Here's the thing, though. Despite the game being a cast-iron masterpiece, this reaction was something of a surprise to me. Or rather, it was a surprise precisely because the game was a cast-iron masterpiece. In truth, a couple of weeks ago I wasn't really aching to head back to Ocarina of Time after all these years. I kind of dreaded having to slog through an echoing, once-great game and summon a thousand words of measured reverence afterwards.

Thankfully I had forgotten two things. The first is that I am an idiot, which means that I had failed to realise that any chance to replay a Zelda should be leapt at. And secondly, it turns out that I'd forgotten exactly what kind of masterpiece Ocarina of Time is. And along with that last point - and we'll get to this properly in a bit - I hadn't realised that there's a secret ingredient to this specific remake that has proved absolutely essential to its greatness, and that has nothing at all to do with the code running on the Switch 2.

Let's deal with remake duties here. This is more or less the game that people played back in 1998. The beats of the adventure, with Link travelling between different eras of Hyrule in order to defeat Ganon, remain the same. You still start in Kokiri Forest and you still ride Epona over the fence at Lon Lon Ranch in one of the great heart-racing, skin-prickling moments in all of art. If you're stuck in a dungeon, you can almost always use an existing guide from the N64 game to work your way through it. The game world is still broken up into little chunks that fade out and in as you move between them. And each game still begins with that unskippably evocative intro that has Link and Epona dashing over a misty hill with the moon behind them, Zelda meets Susan Cooper.

Changes though? For one thing the whole game's been updated with modern graphics, and has ditched any and all fixed cameras for a modern system of movement on one thumbstick and camera on the other. One example: Hyrule Castle Town, in my memory at least, always had a central camera and you would pivot about its streets as if you were a horse on a circus merry-go-round.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

Now it's pure Frozen territory, cobbled paths racing off in every direction and you can explore them with the camera rushing behind you. The game's spaces feel less like elaborate machines that you were a mechanical part of, and more like video game spaces. Yes, from the way I've phrased that I now see that something of a trade-off has taken place here. I loved that sense you got in early 3D games that the whole thing was a clever practical trick that was forever almost about to collapse in on itself, but anyway! The new Ocarina is a game you can show kids who weren't alive in 1998 and they will feel at home more quickly.

Sometimes the graphical update is really wonderful. The route to Zora's Domain, which I barely remember in the original Ocarina, is now a lovely scramble over cliffs and arcing crags. A bold smattering of 1990s Nickelodeon colours and glossy textures, meanwhile, makes Jabu Jabu's Belly a cross between a pre-millennium rave and a modern soft play.

My favourite locations of all, however, are two of the mid-game dungeons. The Water Temple is now a drowned Art Nouveau palace that you could easily imagine Captain Nemo knocking around in. And the Forest Temple, which is my absolute favourite Zelda dungeon of all time, is a parquet-floored murder mansion that's been overtaken by trees. Dark wood-panelled corridors and weird bits of church sticking out of the foliage. It's the kind of place you'd hear a weird crime podcast about.

Trade-offs, however. My wife, a huge fan of the original game, would wander in and out as I played, and often felt the game she remembered was a little more characterful in its visuals. The moment you fight Dark Link, for example, has lost a little of its glitchy liminality, although the staging, with an old tree in the middle of a vast smoky room, is still wonderfully strange. Towards the end of the game, with the trip into Gerudo territory, you could also occasionally be forgiven for wondering if you'd stepped into one of a dozen third-person Unreal games in development at the moment. It's pleasant to look at, but it sometimes doesn't look specifically like Zelda anymore.

All that, and some strange character models that inevitably I learned to love, don't really matter very much, however. Not least because a handful of clever tweaks elsewhere mean that Ocarina now races along at an astonishing clip. And all this with a careful paring back of intrusions from Navi the fairy and the owl, who were both there in the original game to help move you along swiftly in the first place.

These tweaks are all pretty great. Link now has a jump button, which removes the original game's contextual jumps from the equation, and makes the thundering jump attack even more pleasing to pull off. Even better, in a loan from the 3DS remake of Ocarina, you can swap out usable items using a trigger mini-menu, and you can change boots and whatever you had on your head with some of the directional face buttons.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

This doesn't sound like much, but it's quietly transformative in the way that the best updates are. Take the Water Temple. This is the stuff of memes in terms of difficulty and the patience required in navigating an environment that can be flooded up to three different levels. But now, as on the 3DS, you can enjoy it without having to slip into the menu every few steps to add your iron boots or remove them.

And this in turn means that a dungeon I had been really dreading turned out to be a dungeon that revealed itself via experimentation. I would change the water level and see what options I now had, think about the relationship between spaces I could reach and spaces I could not, all without needing to muddle about in menus and interrupt the flow of things. Flow is the word in fact: a simple UI and item-management tweak has given a legendary Zelda dungeon its perfect pace and sense of revelation.

Alongside tweaks like that which I noticed - oh, it's easier to equip the Hookshot - are no doubt hundreds of little things I didn't notice. I suspect there's a lot more gentle direction prompting built into places like the Water Temple, while elsewhere, in the Forest Temple, for example, I suspected that some of the backtracking had been removed. Individual item placements have been changed around perhaps, and there are generous tweaks like a wallet that holds more rupees from the off. For me at least, all of these tweaks had several things in common: they improved the game without removing or altering anything that was particularly meaningful about the original, and, also, I struggled to confidently spot them.

I did try to spot them for a while. And I measured up what I was playing against my memory, which is always wonky in the first place. Hyrule Field feels smaller now, but it's still thrilling to race across. I remember Epona entering the game sooner, or maybe I just remember the idea of a horse in a Zelda game being a huge, attention-holding deal. I thought a favourite boss involving oil paintings came much later, but again, I had just shifted it to the third act because of its original impact on me.

But this gives way over time to the most important thing about Ocarina of Time, I think, and the reason why this remake has such an emotional impact on people like me. This isn't just another Zelda with an ingenious overworld. It's a Zelda game that's even more preoccupied with time than ever before. And this is because time unfolds within the game, via a central mechanic that takes Hyrule seven years into the future, transforming Link from a child to an adult - and then allows you to go back again.

To play a game like this, a game that is about this stuff, after a period of almost thirty years away, gives your imagination and memory a kind of IMAX treatment. I realised that not only is this a game about the passage of time and the way that the world looks different when you're young to when you're a bit older - I had never really realised that adult Link goes through variations of the same dungeons that young Link went through, but now they're all just a bit harder and more consequential - it's also the kind of game that a lot of players have knowingly or unknowingly measured parts of their lives by.

1 of 8

Caption

Attribution

This time, when I reached the first Fairy Fountain, for example, I remembered that my wife had walked down the aisle to this music - about half the registry office recognised the tune with a shiver of laughter, incidentally. Then there's the Water Temple, which has become cultural shorthand for a challenge that is really not screwing around. How many awful things had I faced in life by first conjuring the spirit of Link about to enter this place.

There's that first arrival in Hyrule Field, which is both a promise of everything that games were about to become in 1998 and that fleeting moment in childhood where the boundaries suddenly change. This game doesn't just send me back into my memories, then. It puts me back in conversation with all the people I have known who have ever loved it. I play it now and think I'm talking to my friend who played it at university, or my wife who loved it long before we met.

Was it always this good? Were the dungeons always so complex and challenging, but also so playful, so coherent? Were the bosses always driven by interesting ideas and drama and humour rather than difficulty? Was the world always so rich with minor characters who linger in the mind - the accordion player in the windmill, the gravedigger who has his own tour he'd really like you to try out? It's impossible for me to say at this point. This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday. If you're new to Zelda and you're coming to this game fresh, you're going to love it. Someone, somewhere, is about to play a game so special for the first time that they need to call up their friend and tell them all about it. But if you're returning to this game? Well, somehow you'll find that you're still coming to it fresh.

My dad always said that you should read Don Quixote three times in your life, and I only recently realised that he meant that the book changes because you change. So. When I got to the Deku Tree back at the start of Ocarina a few weeks ago, and I completed the dungeon and watched the impossible vision of the Deku Tree dying of weariness? I remembered that the first time I'd been here, almost thirty years ago, I couldn't help but identify with Link, freshly gifted a sword and shield, one dungeon down, ready for whatever came next. This time, I think, I was closer to identifying with the Deku Tree.

And here's the important part: this wasn't a depressing thought. It just meant that I had taken the long route to reach this point, and this astonishing game had taken the long route too. And yet we arrived at this point together, and together we were transformed. And that's really why any of this video game stuff matters.

A copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was provided for this review by Nintendo.

title: Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement
author: Adam Feldman
content:
On May 21, 2026, Justice Elena Kagan did something she had never done in nearly 16 years on the Supreme Court: she dissented alone in a signed decision. The case, Havana Docks v. Royal Caribbean Cruises, concerned whether cruise lines could face liability for using Cuban docks confiscated decades earlier. Eight justices, including Kagan’s liberal colleagues Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, sided against the cruise lines. Kagan thought the majority had misunderstood a basic principle of property law: the interest originally confiscated had expired long before the cruise ships arrived.

The solitary dissent was unusual for a justice who has spent much of her tenure avoiding separate opinions. At a judicial conference in July 2025, Kagan observed that the court “speaks best when it speaks as a court,” and acknowledged that she sometimes drafts dissents only to decide against publishing them.

Kagan’s professional background is also unusual. She is the only current justice who arrived at the Supreme Court without previously serving as a judge. Before her appointment in 2010, she had been a law professor, dean of Harvard Law School, a White House adviser, and solicitor general of the United States. Her career was therefore shaped substantially by institutions in which persuasion, negotiation, and managing competing perspectives are routine.

But how much does this explain her jurisprudence? Ideological measures generally place Kagan to the right of her liberal colleagues, and her voting record contains meaningful differences from Sotomayor’s and Jackson’s. Yet those differences are far from uniform, and Kagan’s reluctance to write separately persists even when she reaches precisely the same result as her colleagues.

Understanding Kagan therefore requires examining not only how she votes, but how she chooses to agree and disagree.

How liberal Is Kagan?

Kagan has generally occupied a position to the right of the other liberal justices in measures of Supreme Court ideology. But the distance between them depends considerably on how ideology is measured, which cases are examined, and when the comparison is made.

The best-known measure is the Martin–Quinn score, which estimates the justices’ ideological positions from their voting patterns over time. In the 2024-25 term, Kagan’s score was −1.85, compared with −2.80 for Jackson and −4.19 for Sotomayor. Kagan was thus the rightmost of the three liberals, although she remained substantially to the left of the court’s median justice, Amy Coney Barrett, whose score was +0.53. The estimates for Jackson and Kagan had been closer in earlier terms (and, in fact, Jackson was initially positioned slightly to Kagan’s right).

The scores capture something revealing about how the justices vote, but they do not directly measure the substance of their legal reasoning or their willingness to compromise. Nor does a justice’s location relative to the other liberals necessarily reveal whether her own jurisprudence has changed. Martin–Quinn estimates are relative positions derived from voting coalitions, and those coalitions are themselves influenced by the court’s membership and docket.

The voting record offers a more concrete comparison. During the 2010–2021 terms, there were 56 contested decisions in which Kagan joined the majority while Sotomayor dissented, compared with just 19 in which their positions were reversed. Kagan was nearly three times as likely to be on the prevailing side when the two disagreed. That is a substantial difference, although it does not establish that every disagreement reflected an ideological division.

Justice Stephen Breyer, long considered a moderate liberal on the court, provides a useful point of reference. During their overlapping time on the court, Kagan joined the majority without Breyer 41 times, while Breyer joined the majority without Kagan 31 times. The more balanced relationship suggests that Kagan’s historical voting behavior often resembled Breyer’s more closely than Sotomayor’s.

The picture has changed since Jackson joined the court in 2022. Across 121 contested decisions in which Kagan and Sotomayor both participated through the 2025 term, they voted on the same side 109 times. Kagan prevailed without Sotomayor seven times, while Sotomayor prevailed without Kagan five times. Their historical difference in majority participation has thus narrowed dramatically.

The convergence is particularly visible in closely divided cases. Of 82 decisions decided 5–4 or 6–3 in which Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson all participated, the three liberals voted together in 71. When the court divided most sharply, Kagan usually found herself alongside her liberal colleagues rather than occupying a position between the liberal and conservative wings.

There are then two different stories in the numbers. Over much of her tenure, Kagan was more likely than Sotomayor to support outcomes favored by conservative justices. More recently, that distinction has diminished, particularly in closely divided cases. Whether this reflects a change in Kagan’s jurisprudence or the changing opportunities for cross-ideological agreement remains uncertain.

The cases in which she breaks with her liberal colleagues offer a way to examine that distinction more closely.

When Kagan breaks with the liberals

One way to identify a comparatively moderate justice is to examine how frequently she votes with colleagues across the ideological divide. By that measure, Kagan has demonstrated considerable independence from her liberal colleagues.

Across 26 terms, Kagan was the only liberal voting alongside conservative justices in 27 contested decisions, approximately 5.3% of her non-unanimous votes. Sotomayor occupied that position in 18 decisions, or 3.4%. Yet Breyer did so in 29 cases, representing 7.1% of his contested votes during the years he served alongside Kagan. When he was on the court, Breyer, rather than Kagan, was more likely to separate from the other liberals in that way.

The pattern becomes even more interesting with Jackson’s arrival. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan was the sole liberal voting with conservatives in nine contested cases, compared with ten for Jackson (though this frequency has decreased) and just two for Sotomayor. Jackson’s cross-ideological votes were evenly divided between joining majorities and dissents, while Kagan’s predominantly placed her in the majority. Thus, even when two justices cross ideological lines with similar frequency, they may not be doing the same thing.

These voting coalitions also raise a question about Kagan’s reputation as a consensus-builder. Does she actually attract more conservative support when writing for the court?

The analysis provides surprisingly little evidence that she does. Of Kagan’s 47 majority opinions in contested decisions, 27 attracted at least three conservative votes. Sotomayor achieved the same result in 30 of her 49 contested majority opinions. Their records are then similar, suggesting that Kagan’s reputation for building agreement is not necessarily reflected in a distinctive ability to assemble ideologically diverse majorities.

The individual cases also complicate the idea that Kagan’s departures from the liberal wing are simply strategic compromises. In 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas, for example, Kagan wrote for six justices, including five conservatives, holding that the Constitution does not require states to recognize an insanity defense based on a defendant’s inability to distinguish right from wrong. Breyer, joined by Ginsburg and Sotomayor, dissented. Kagan emphasized the historical diversity of insanity rules and the latitude afforded to state legislatures; Breyer saw Kansas’s approach as eliminating a fundamental protection deeply rooted in criminal law.

Four years later, Pulsifer v. United States presented a dispute over the meaning of a single conjunction in a federal sentencing statute. Kagan wrote for a six-justice majority, including five conservatives, adopting a reading that restricted defendants’ eligibility for relief from mandatory minimum sentences. Gorsuch dissented, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, favoring an interpretation that would have made relief more widely available.

Neither case is easily explained as Kagan merely accommodating conservative colleagues and both show substantive disagreements over the meaning of legal rules, with significant consequences for criminal defendants.

These decisions also show why ideological distance and judicial method cannot be treated as interchangeable. Kagan’s cross-ideological votes sometimes reflect legal commitments that produce outcomes different from those favored by her liberal colleagues. They also suggest that her willingness to build agreement does not automatically lead her toward the narrowest available resolution.

If Kagan is not consistently more successful than Sotomayor at attracting conservative votes, the more distinctive feature of her jurisprudence may lie elsewhere: what she does after reaching agreement, and particularly when she decides that a disagreement warrants an opinion of her own.

The art of agreement: choosing when to write

The most distinctive feature of Kagan’s judicial behavior may have less to do with how she votes than with how she expresses agreement. During her 16 terms on the court, Kagan authored just 18 concurrences in signed decisions, compared with 81 for Sotomayor. Breyer, often described as an institutionally minded pragmatist, also wrote concurrences at more than twice Kagan’s rate during their overlapping service. Jackson has been considerably more prolific in her shorter tenure. Kagan’s comparative restraint is therefore striking even among justices who share many of her substantive positions.

The difference becomes even more revealing when the comparison is limited to cases in which the justices reached exactly the same outcome. Between 2010 and 2021, Kagan and Sotomayor both supported a conservative-authored majority opinion in 93 contested decisions. Sotomayor wrote separately in 13 of those cases; Kagan did so in just one. The difference is difficult to explain through ideology or case selection alone: the two justices were participating in the same decisions, agreeing with the same majorities, yet approaching the question of whether to write separately very differently.

The distinction has narrowed somewhat in recent years, but it has not vanished. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan wrote separately in three of 38 conservative-authored majorities she shared with Sotomayor, compared with five for Sotomayor. In 29 comparable cases involving Kagan and Jackson, Kagan wrote separately twice and Jackson eight times. These samples are smaller, but they reinforce the larger finding that Kagan is particularly reluctant to add her individual voice to an outcome she already supports.

Kagan herself has offered a remarkably candid explanation for this. Speaking at the 9th Circuit Judicial Conference in July 2025, she described the Supreme Court as an institution whose opinions should communicate a collective judgment. She acknowledged that producing a single institutional voice requires “a little bit of flexibility and compromise.” Separate opinions, she suggested, can complicate the law by presenting competing explanations of what the court has supposedly decided.

Yet Kagan’s restraint should not be mistaken for unqualified agreement. In 2024’s United States v. Rahimi, she joined Roberts’ majority upholding a federal restriction on firearm possession by individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders. She also joined Sotomayor’s concurrence, which defended the majority’s application of New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen while reiterating their disagreement with that earlier Second Amendment decision holding there to be a constitutional right to carry a firearm. Jackson wrote her own concurrence addressing the difficulties lower courts had encountered applying Bruen. All three liberals agreed with the outcome, but their choices about authorship differed.

A similar pattern appeared in 2023’s National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, in which the court rejected an argument by pork producers that a law violated the Constitution by regulating the pork industry outside of California. Kagan joined Sotomayor’s separate opinion explaining why they agreed with the judgment without embracing portions of Gorsuch’s reasoning that threatened to alter the established constitutional framework. Kagan was willing to register a qualification, but she did so by joining a colleague’s opinion rather than writing another.

These distinctions again complicate the portrayal of Kagan as a consensus-builder. The data do not show that she consistently attracts more conservative support to her own majority opinions than Sotomayor does. They show something different: Kagan is considerably more selective about articulating separate disagreements when she already supports the court’s disposition. That behavior may preserve a clearer institutional message, but it also leaves fewer public indication of her reservations about particular decisions.

The difference matters when interpreting Kagan’s ideological position. A justice who joins an opinion without writing separately may appear closer to its author than one who publishes a concurrence, even when both share the same substantive objection. Kagan’s record suggests the absence of a separate opinion can reflect a decision about judicial expression rather than any lack of disagreement.

The limits of agreement: textualism, precedent, and dissent

Kagan’s willingness to work across ideological lines has never meant avoiding deep disagreements with the court’s conservatives. Some of her sharpest opinions have challenged not only their conclusions but also their fidelity to the interpretive principles they profess to follow.

In a 2015 lecture at Harvard Law School honoring Antonin Scalia, Kagan famously remarked, “We’re all textualists now.” The observation acknowledged Scalia’s influence on statutory interpretation, including among justices who did not share his ideological commitments. Seven years later, in her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, Kagan explicitly revisited that statement: “It seems I was wrong.”

Her objection concerned the majority’s use of the major questions doctrine to restrict the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act. Kagan argued that the court had departed from ordinary statutory interpretation by demanding an unusually clear congressional authorization for agency action of substantial economic or political significance. In her account, the conservative majority’s claimed commitment to textualism yielded when the statutory text pointed toward an outcome it disfavored.

The exchange is revealing because Kagan was challenging the majority from within a methodology often associated with conservative jurisprudence. Her embrace of textualism did not entail agreement with the conservatives about what particular statutes meant, much less about how much authority courts should exercise over Congress and administrative agencies.

That distinction became even clearer in 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Writing for the three liberals, subject to Jackson’s recusal in one of the consolidated cases, Kagan defended Chevron deference (deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes) against the majority’s decision to overrule it. Her argument rested on statutory interpretation, congressional allocation of authority, administrative expertise, and the importance of precedent (a common theme for her). Textualism, in Kagan’s jurisprudence, does not necessarily require courts to resolve every statutory ambiguity without deference to an agency authorized to administer the law.

The same institutional concerns appear in her criticism of the court’s emergency docket. In Trump v. Wilcox, Kagan dissented from an order permitting the administration, pending further litigation, to remove officials from independent agencies. Joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, she objected both to the treatment of longstanding precedent and to the use of an expedited proceeding to alter the practical operation of existing law without ordinary briefing and argument.

These opinions provide an important counterweight to Kagan’s reputation for accommodation. Her restraint in writing separately does not preclude forceful disagreement when she believes the court has departed from established interpretive or institutional principles. Nor does that pattern necessarily distinguish her substantive positions from those of Sotomayor and Jackson, who joined these dissents.

The recurring question is therefore not simply whether Kagan is willing to compromise but where she draws the line between disagreements she can accommodate and those that she considers important enough to articulate publicly.

Kagan’s place on the changing court

Sixteen years of decisions reveal a justice whose reputation for moderation captures only part of her judicial behavior. Kagan has historically been more willing than Sotomayor to join conservative-supported outcomes, and some of those differences reflect genuine disagreements about the law. Yet the gap has narrowed considerably in recent terms, particularly in cases that divide the court along ideological lines.

What distinguishes Kagan more consistently is her approach to disagreement. She is not uniquely successful at attracting conservative votes to her majority opinions. Rather, she is unusually reluctant to write separately when she can support an existing opinion, even in cases where her liberal colleagues reach the same result but feel compelled to explain their reservations. Her willingness to join another justice’s concurrence further complicates any assumption that silence necessarily signifies agreement.

The distinction has become more consequential as the court has moved rightward. Kagan’s opportunities to assemble majorities across ideological lines have diminished, while her dissents in disputes over administrative authority, precedent, and institutional power have become an increasingly public part of her jurisprudence.

Whether those patterns reflect a conscious strategy, enduring professional instincts, or some combination of the two cannot be determined from voting records alone. But the comparisons suggest that understanding Kagan requires looking beyond where she falls on an ideological scale. Her place on the court is defined both by the legal positions she takes and by the choices she makes about when – and how – to express them.

Recommended Citation: Adam Feldman, Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 5, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/who-is-elena-kagan-ideology-strategy-and-the-art-of-disagreement/

title: National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
In the summer of 1972, President Nixon’s reelection campaign financed the break-in at the Watergate complex with over $500,000 of campaign funds.1 Still, corrupt donors continued to fill the campaign’s coffers, allegedly using the Republican National Committee as a pass-through to avoid public scrutiny.2 After the Watergate hearings, Congress amended the Federal Election Campaign Act3 (FECA) in 1974, creating an enforcement agency, the FEC, and capping what campaigns, parties, and individuals could spend on or contribute to election-related activities.4 In a 2001 case known as Colorado II,5 the Supreme Court upheld FECA’s cap on a political party’s coordinated campaign expenditures.6 Coordinated expenditures — money spent “in cooperation, consultation or concert with, or at the request or suggestion of, a candidate”7 — were treated functionally as “contributions” because they offset a campaign’s expenses just like gifts of cash.8 Applying “closely drawn” scrutiny,9 Colorado II held that political-party coordinated-expenditure limits were sufficiently tailored to the important government interest of “combating political corruption.”10

Last Term, in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC11 (NRSC), a group of plaintiffs including Vice President J.D. Vance again challenged the constitutionality of political-party coordinated-expenditure restrictions under the First Amendment.12 This time, the petitioners had the Court’s jurisprudential trajectory, if not its precedent, on their side. The Roberts Court has slowly but inexorably rolled back FECA’s remaining campaign finance limitations.13 NRSC marked the next chapter in this project, freeing political parties to spend unlimited amounts in coordination with campaigns.14 Perhaps more foundationally, however, NRSC effected an unstated but avulsive change in the Court’s campaign finance jurisprudence by collapsing the doctrinal treatment of contributions and expenditures, thereby extending speech-like protection to all money in politics. This categorical treatment of money mischaracterizes the theoretical relationship between speech and money and protects a party’s bill-paying as equivalent to speech.

Four days before the 2022 midterm election, the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), then–Senate candidate Vance, and then-Representative Steve Chabot sued the FEC and its commissioners, seeking to enjoin them from enforcing FECA’s coordinated-expenditure limits.15 Pursuant to section 310 of FECA, the plaintiffs moved to certify a question of the statute’s constitutionality to the en banc Sixth Circuit.16 Judge Cole of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Ohio ruled that the plaintiffs had standing and raised a nonfrivolous issue, even if “Colorado II squarely applie[d].”17 Judge Cole certified the constitutional question as proposed by the plaintiffs and declined to certify “legislative facts” that he deemed more appropriate for judicial notice.18

The Sixth Circuit, self-aware of its role as a “warm-up for eventual Supreme Court review,”19 answered the certified question in favor of the FEC.20 Chief Judge Sutton,21 writing for the en banc court, held that Colorado II controlled.22 His opinion acknowledged that campaign finance doctrine had shifted since Colorado II but concluded that “it remains the Court’s job, not ours, to overrule it.”23 Some of the Chief Judge’s colleagues went a step further. Judge Thapar, writing a concurrence in name only, reasoned that First Amendment jurisprudence should follow New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen’s24 two-step history and tradition analysis.25 Judge Bush, answering the history-and-tradition call, concurred separately, contending that the history showed “no exception relevantly similar to the restriction at issue here.”26 Judge Readler dissented, claiming that the Sixth Circuit should not have been bound by a “largely obsolete precedent.”27 Judge Stranch, responding to her colleagues’ assorted attacks on Colorado II, concurred in the judgment and fervently defended the constitutionality of FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits.28 With pointed brevity, Judge Bloomekatz wrote a two-sentence concurrence in the judgment noting that Colorado II remains binding precedent.29 As the Sixth Circuit predicted, the Supreme Court granted certiorari.30

Writing for the Court’s six conservative Justices, Justice Kavanaugh31 began by quoting Buckley v. Valeo,32 the Court’s foundational campaign finance opinion from 1976.33 A brief excursus on Buckley sets the stage for Justice Kavanaugh’s opinion: Buckley, which struck down FECA’s limits on independent expenditures, held that campaign expenditures and contributions implicated different First Amendment interests and that restrictions thereon were subject to different tiers of scrutiny.34 “[B]ecause virtually every means of communicating ideas in today’s mass society requires the expenditure of money,”35 the Buckley Court treated campaign expenditures as pure speech and thus subjected expenditure restrictions to “exacting scrutiny.”36 By contrast, contributions were primarily valuable for their expressive and associative content, not any speech inherent in gifts of money.37 Thus, the Court applied a less rigorous “closely drawn” scrutiny to FECA’s contribution restrictions and upheld them, regardless of whether the contribution was money or coordinated spending.38

In NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh ignored Colorado II’s functional characterization of coordinated expenditures as contributions. “[S]pending limits,” he wrote in the opinion’s opening paragraph, “necessarily abridge political parties’ freedom of speech.”39 Indeed, Justice Kavanaugh never referenced Colorado II’s central premise, that FECA treats coordinated expenditures as contributions.40 Instead, Justice Kavanaugh characterized the regulated transactions from the party’s perspective as spender rather than from the campaign’s perspective as recipient.41 Classified as a limit on spending rather than on contributions, FECA’s cap on coordinated party expenditures seems to burden the pure speech that Buckley protected.

Nevertheless — and without explaining the discrepancy — Justice Kavanaugh applied “closely drawn” scrutiny, the test that Buckley and Colorado II described as appropriate for limits on contributions.42 Recent Court precedent, he noted, had raised the threshold for what kind of tailoring counts as “closely drawn.”43 Thus, Justice Kavanaugh said, “we need not dwell on any subtle differences between the two tests.”44 Although the difference between “strict” and “closely drawn” scrutiny was decisive in Buckley, Justice Kavanaugh posited that “the question of which test to apply here is ultimately academic,” as both tests assess the government’s asserted interest in limiting speech and the fit between the interest and those limits.45

Justice Kavanaugh then rejected three hypothetical government interests for restricting campaign finance before turning to the only interest asserted by the Court-appointed amicus: preventing quid pro quo corruption or the appearance thereof.46 The theory of political-party coordinated-expenditure corruption posits that a corrupt donor would circumvent their individual contribution limits by donating to the party in the expectation, or on the explicit promise, that the money would be passed on to the campaign.47 Preventing corrupt actors from circumventing the base contribution limits is sufficiently important to justify burdening First Amendment speech, but a permissible restriction must be “closely drawn,”48 “narrowly tailored,”49 and “necessary for the interest it seeks to protect.”50

Where Colorado II applied only deferential review to the question of fit, later cases like McCutcheon v. FEC51 and FEC v. Ted Cruz for Senate52 sharpened the Court’s assessment of campaign finance tailoring.53 Thus, Justice Kavanaugh concluded that two less restrictive alternatives — earmarking and disclosure laws — made FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure restrictions unnecessary.54 Earmarking laws already make it illegal to circumvent base limits with contributions “directed through an intermediary or conduit.”55 Furthermore, FECA’s disclosure requirements obligate political parties and candidates to publicly disclose both expenditures and contributions, including coordinated expenditures.56 That transparency, according to the Court, arms the public and FEC with enough information to enforce earmarking rules.57 In order to prevent quid pro quo corruption, an individual’s base contribution limits are, according to Justice Kavanaugh, a first layer of prophylaxis; earmarking and disclosure requirements are a second and third layer; as a fourth layer of prophylaxis, FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits were deemed “disproportionate”58 and not “necessary.”59

Nor would stare decisis save FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limits. Justice Kavanaugh considered “the egregiousness of the precedent’s error, the jurisprudential and real-world effects of the decision, and any cognizable reliance interests,”60 and concluded that all three factors militated in favor of overturning Colorado II.61 To demonstrate the egregiousness of Colorado II’s error, Justice Kavanaugh pointed to Justice Thomas’s “persuasive” 2001 dissent.62 As for real-world effects, Justice Kavanaugh noted that political parties have been relegated to “second-tier status” relative to outside groups like super PACs.63 Overruling Colorado II, he reasoned, would level the field.64 Finally, Justice Kavanaugh discounted any reliance that outside groups have in their relative advantage over parties without considering the differential effect such a ruling would have between national parties.65

Justice Kagan dissented.66 She did not dispute Justice Kavanaugh’s characterization of the political-party coordinated-expenditure limit as burdening pure speech or his description of the appropriate level of scrutiny. Instead, she addressed the granularities of campaign finance, showing how a motivated donor could use parties and their joint fundraising committees to circumvent the base contribution limit.67 Joint fundraising committees represent a candidate’s campaign, the relevant national party, and each of the fifty state parties, allowing a donor to combine each of his maximum donations into a single check ($7,000 to the campaign, $44,300 to the national party, and $10,000 to each of the state parties, totaling $551,300).68 As Justice Kagan articulated, donations to a hypothetical joint committee, the “John Smith Victory Fund,” require no earmarking to communicate a preferred candidate.69 The joint committee then disburses the contribution maximums to the national and state parties, which, within a few days, transfer that money back to the national party.70 Under Colorado II, the national party was limited in how much it could spend in coordination with John Smith’s campaign.71 Now, all $551,300 is potentially available to pay any of a campaign’s bills — from media spending to plumbing — completing the donor’s circumvention of the $7,000 base contribution limit.72 In Justice Kagan’s view, then, FECA’s political-party coordinated-expenditure limitations appropriately prevented circumvention of the base limit and should have passed the fit test “with flying colors.”73

With the Roberts Court’s long process of campaign finance deregulation nearly at a close, it is worth reflecting on the unstated doctrinal evolution effectuated since Buckley: the collapse of any practical distinction between contributions and expenditures. In NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh confused the descriptive boundary between the two and further sharpened “closely drawn” scrutiny so that it approaches strict scrutiny. First, a contribution can be formalistically redescribed from the perspective of the donor, making it appear like an expenditure. And second, even if the Court chooses to apply “closely drawn” scrutiny, it will find any less restrictive means dispositive of a statute’s constitutionality. Although Justice Kavanaugh insisted that his opinion “does not address the statutory limits on coordinated expenditures by outside groups,” little in his logic is specific to political parties.74 Through this descriptive and doctrinal two-step, Justice Kavanaugh effectively erased any practical distinction between contributions and expenditures, thereby paving the way for all money in politics to receive categorical protection as pure speech. But money cannot be constitutionally protected speech in all circumstances. Money’s symbolic nature forecloses such a categorical treatment.

From a doctrinal perspective, the outcome in NRSC is not all that surprising. Since its inception, the contribution-expenditure dichotomy has been criticized for imperfectly answering whether a particular transaction amounts to speech.75 Most notably, several Justices have levied categorical criticisms, suggesting that money either always or never amounts to constitutionally protected speech.76 Indeed, Justice Thomas has long called for Buckley’s distinction between contributions and expenditures to be overruled.77 Over the last decade, the Court has repeatedly struck down FECA provisions that restricted contributions or their functional equivalents like coordinated expenditures.78 Along the way, the Court has gradually redescribed Buckley’s “closely drawn” scrutiny such that it now nearly resembles strict scrutiny. In Colorado II, the Court said that “closely drawn” scrutiny does not require overturning contribution limits for “unskillful tailoring.”79 In McCutcheon, however, the Court called the standard “lesser but still ‘rigorous’” relative to strict scrutiny.80 And in NRSC, Justice Kavanaugh further modified that description, labeling the Court’s review only “nominally ‘lesser but still rigorous.’”81 If, as Justice Kavanaugh wrote, the difference between strict and “closely drawn” scrutiny is “subtle” and ultimately “academic,” then both contributions and expenditures are, for practical purposes, protected like pure speech under the First Amendment.82 By treating contributions and expenditures with the same level of review, the Court has accomplished Justice Thomas’s goal in effect if not in name and extended the full protection of the First Amendment to all money in politics.

But money, standing alone, is not communicative; rather, it adopts symbolic meaning from a transaction and its context.83 To give more analytical content to the relationship between money and speech, we can identify two communicative components in every use of money. First, assuming no coercion, the fact of transaction makes an expression of value.84 That is, every free use of money contains the implied statement from each participant, “this is worth it to me.” That expression of value is present in every transaction and so, assuming that not every transaction is constitutionally protected speech, it cannot be sufficient to make a particular transaction constitutionally protected speech. The second communicative component of money relates to the underlying substance of a transaction. Money, in this way, symbolically adopts some meaning from the exchanged good. Whereas the expression of value is scalar, suggesting how much something is worth, the substantive component is directional, communicating, with enough context, the dimensions along which something has worth. Buying a sandwich, for instance, communicates something — perhaps a buyer’s hunger, her ethical commitment to veganism, or her generosity in feeding her companion — but its substantive meaning relies on more than the underlying good.85 That is, money becomes speech only through its context, not just its existence.

In NRSC, however, Justice Kavanaugh did not endeavor to assess what meaning, if any, was actually communicated by the regulated transactions.86 Instead, he treated money categorically, eschewing any attempt to determine whether the regulated transactions communicated something beyond the universal expression of value, “this is worth it to me.” Indeed, approximately three percent of the committees’ coordinated spending was, facially, not related to underlying political speech.87 The substantive component of those transactions — perhaps communicating a need for electricity or more campaign staffers — was decidedly not sacred political speech. But the other ninety-seven percent of transactions, “relate[d] to the ‘political advertising’” of Republican campaigns,88 was more difficult to assess. What, if anything, does it communicate for the NRSC to fund the speech of the campaigns it supports? Consider, for example, an email exchange regarding a coordinated expenditure between then–Senate candidate Vance’s campaign and the NRSC.89 After working with a media agency to plan, film, and edit a television commercial, Vance’s campaign forwarded the invoice to the NRSC for payment.90 The NRSC simply responded, “Received. Will process.”91 Does paying the campaign’s bill convert the advertisement into the NRSC’s own speech? This comment does not purport to offer an answer to such a difficult question. Perhaps symbolic speech doctrine could provide a more careful and accurate measure of when money symbolically adopts any underlying speech.92

But the Court has given up on this difficult, functional task. One could imagine an as-applied version of NRSC that threads this needle.93 To the extent that the NRSC was actually expressing its own speech, perhaps the coordination restrictions are poorly fitted to the government’s interest in preventing corruption. Justices Kavanaugh and Kagan would, presumably, still disagree on this “legally quite narrow” question.94 But whether the NRSC was speaking in the first place is knowable only by analyzing the communicative components of the transaction in question. Instead, the Court categorically links payment to speech, giving undue protection to bill-paying as speech.

The conclusion that money is speech has been criticized before,95 but NRSC thrusts it back into the spotlight by collapsing the doctrinal treatment of campaign expenditures and contributions. Thus, money receives categorical, speech-like constitutional protection, regardless of its use. Although the Court did not say as much in NRSC, the outcome is inevitable under Justice Kavanaugh’s logic. Indeed, at oral argument, Justice Kavanaugh seemed interested in discussing what little remains of FECA’s campaign finance restrictions.96 But such a categorical treatment of money is incongruous with the symbolic nature of money itself, which draws its speech-like meaning from the underlying substance of a given transaction. In NRSC, the Court rejected any factual analysis of the regulated transactions, categorically treating money in politics as speech. It did so without a theory of money’s relation to speech and erroneously concluded that a political party always speaks when it pays for its campaigns.

title: Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution
author: Steven Gow Calabresi
content:
A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)”

***

Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s new book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

First, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.)

But Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer blindly to the political process. Justice Alito recognizes that judicial restraint where the Supreme Court has wrongly deferred to the political process is unconstitutional under Article III and has produced tragic results in cases like Plessy v. Ferguson, in which the court ratified Jim Crow race discrimination by the political branches of the government, or Korematsu v. United States, in which the court ratified President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s internment of over 100,000 innocent Japanese American citizens. In those cases the Supreme Court erred by not enforcing the Constitution. Yet at other times it has erred by being judicially activist as in Dred Scott v. Sanford or Lochner v. New York or Roe v. Wade. As Justice Alito teaches us, the Supreme Court should be neither judicially activist nor judicially restrained. It should uphold constitutional laws and strike down unconstitutional laws. This is what the rule of law is all about.

Justice Alito is equally and rightly skeptical of the notion that judges should be Dworkinian natural rights theorists, progressive constitutionalists like Chief Justice Earl Warren, or implementers of Catholic natural law as is argued by Harvard Law School Professor Adrian Vermeule. Indeed, Justice Alito devotes a whole chapter of his book to rejecting the idea that Supreme Court justices should implement natural law. This is because Justice Alito is profoundly aware that the American people during the 237 years from 1789 to 2026 have more knowledge and are thus wiser than is one individual Supreme Court, Supreme Court justice, or academic theorist. Although he does not say this outright, Alito appears to believe that originalist judges should be guided by the four cardinal virtues: 1) practical wisdom; 2) justice; 3) courage; and 4) temperance.

At the same time, Justice Alito is very much a Burkean. What does this mean? It calls to mind one of my favorite works of political philosophy, Friedrich Hayek’s volumes 1, 2, and 3 of Law, Legislation, and Liberty. In that masterpiece, Hayek identifies two forms of social order: planned systems of order like a firm or a military platoon, and spontaneous systems of social order like a language, the free market, or a culture of following the rule of law. No one has ever successfully planned a language, but languages have rules of grammar and a fixed meaning of words, and so a language forms what Hayek calls a spontaneous system of social order.

The Constitution and its amendments are a planned system of order, the words of which are so short and abstract that they have given rise to spontaneous systems of order around them. Thus, the freedom of speech and of the press protects thoughts in a private diary or a letter to a friend even though they are not vocal utterances or made with a printing press. Those words also protect freedom of expression in new technologies like movies, radio, television, or the internet, and they even protect expressive conduct that is not vocal at all like burning the American flag contemptuously at a protest rally.

The advantage of a spontaneous system of order like a language, the free market, or constitutional caselaw is that it harnesses the wisdom of many individuals who are always wiser than is one judge or academic theorist. But the countervailing advantage of the Constitution being a planned system of order is that if constitutional case law drifts too far away from the wonderful Novus Ordo Seclorum plan of the framers, the Supreme Court may overrule such caselaw – even after a century of it having been decided. The bottom line is that in figuring out when to follow the planned order of the Constitution or the spontaneous order of constitutional case law and precedents, a justice must further draw on the four cardinal virtues mentioned earlier – practical wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance.

More controversially, Alito argues that one factor in a good constitutional or statutory interpretation is that it produces good consequences. This is contrary to what Justice Scalia used to tell me when I was his law clerk, which is that if a text he is interpreting coming in is garbage, then the decision going out will also be garbage. Justice Scalia insisted it was not his job to make the law better. This differed from the approach which Judge Robert H. Bork, who I clerked for on the D.C. Circuit, followed. Judge Bork would not rewrite the Constitution or statutes to produce good results, but if there were two equally plausible readings of legal language, Judge Bork, like Justice Alito, would go with the one that produced the best outcomes in his view. I would do the same thing.

Nevertheless, in discussing Supreme Court precedents that he thinks were wrongly decided, Justice Alito can sometimes be too timid (in my opinion) in his criticisms. Perhaps that is because as a Supreme Court justice, he feels constrained in calling for the overruling of clearly incorrect precedents. For example, he criticizes Justice Scalia’s opinion in 2012’s United States v. Jones, in which the court held evidence should be suppressed which was obtained from illegally placing a GPS tracking device on a drug dealer’s car. But in his own dissent in that case Justice Alito failed to call for overruling the exclusionary rule cases on which that decision was based, even though his former boss, Attorney General Ed Meese, had publicly called for the overruling of the exclusionary rule in the 1980’s, and even though Congress passed a federal statute overruling it in the context of Miranda v. Arizona in 1968.

Justice Alito also complains rightly about the banning of religion from the public square, but he concedes in his book that as a justice he had failed to join a Scalia dissent, which called for the complete overruling of Flast v. Cohen, an absurd standing precedent of the Warren court which gave taxpayer standing to ACLU litigants who were offended by local government Christmas and Hannukah displays or displays of the Ten Commandments. And Justice Alito quite rightly criticizes Justice Scalia’s decision weakening the free exercise clause case in Employment Division v. Smith, but he does not call for overruling it. He should do so with pride.

The argument for originalism in constitutional interpretation is the same as the argument Justice Alito makes for textualism in statutory interpretation. Legal texts, be they constitutions, statutes, contracts, wills, or Supreme Court opinions should be given their original public meaning. A judge who interpreted a Supreme Court opinion or a contract according to natural law would be violating the fundamental norms of our legal system. Originalist justices can and should follow non-originalist precedents where not doing so would be disruptive to our legal system. I thus agree with Justice Alito that the Supreme Court should follow, for example, its dormant commerce clause precedents.

There is one final area where I and Justice Alito respectfully disagree. Readers of this site, and of Justice Alito’s book, know that we have different views on same-sex marriage and Obergefell v. Hodges. In his book, Justice Alito responds to me by pointing out, among other things, that same-sex marriage was unheard of for 40,000 years of human history.

I will only add here that 250 years ago, on July 4, 1776, nearly every country in the world had slavery, feudalism was widely practiced, there was a caste system in India, racism and religious persecutions were the norm, women’s rights were suppressed, and the public was adamantly opposed to LGTBQ+ rights. Gordon Wood, the famous historian of the American Founding argued in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution that July 4, 1776 was the most important day in all of human history (other than the days of the birth and death of Jesus) because the Declaration of Independence launched a “New Order of the Ages,” which helped bring millennia of human inequality to an end in Western democracies.

It is true that same-sex civil marriage is a very new idea, but so too, in the historical scale of things, is the end or attempted end of slavery, feudalism, the Hindu caste system, racism, religious persecution, and sexism. I think the sudden rise of same-sex marriage stems from the same American Revolution that began 250 years ago on July 4, 1776.

In any event, Justice Alito is to be commended for writing an exceptionally intellectual and provocative new book. The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not.

Recommended Citation: Steven Gow Calabresi, Justice Alito and the tradition of a written constitution, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 11, 2026, 9:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/justice-alito-and-the-tradition-of-a-written-constitution/

title: This $48 e-paper display can be whatever you want it to be
content:
Skip to content

Seeed Feed

This DIY e-paper display works in two official ecosystems or on your own server.

Credit: Nick Indge

Credit: Nick Indge

One of the most useful gadgets in my kitchen is now a screen that never asks me for anything.

I recently bought a $48 DIY display kit from Seeed Studio (yes, that’s three E’s), developed in collaboration with TRMNL, that lets me display whatever I want, using whichever software ecosystem I prefer.

I previously built something similar by modding a Lenovo ThinkSmart View, which was selling for around $30 on eBay during a liquidation. The Lenovo device was only ever intended for business-to-business video, but it does a decent job of running a fork of LineageOS. Unfortunately, its limited RAM makes it sluggish. So when I came across the TRMNL kit and its e-paper display, I was sold.

I’d have an always-on display that shows me the information I want, with no subscription required. And since the screen populates automatically, I would never have to wrestle with a slow interface.

The Seeed Studio kit and TRMNL ecosystem aren’t trying to compete with products like the recently announced Apple HomeView, a $299 home hub designed to get the whole family interacting with it. If anything, the TRMNL kit is the HomeView’s antithesis. It’s designed to be entirely passive: The e-paper display stays on, cycling through potentially useful information on your desk or in your kitchen, from calendars and weather to news and all sorts of ideas thought up by its community members.

Here’s how it works.

Choosing a path

TRMNL, the platform company, was founded by indie hardware enthusiast Ryan Kulp in 2023. Its first e-paper device launched via crowdfunding in 2024.

Seeed Studio provides the hardware. The established Shenzhen open hardware company is best known for its XIAO microcontroller boards.

In March 2025, Seeed teased an XIAO e-paper panel on social media, prompting a community member to ask whether it could run TRMNL firmware. The question brought the two teams together, and in July 2025, they announced an official partnership to develop a DIY e-paper kit combining Seeed’s hardware designs with TRMNL’s firmware packages.

Seeed designs and manufactures the hardware, while TRMNL maintains the firmware, plugins, and hosted service. But you’ll still need to make some decisions about how to set up the kit. There are three ways to get it running, depending on your budget and how comfortable you are with managing software yourself.

The stock TRMNL setup connects you with the company’s “BYOD ecosystem” (bring your own device), letting you use trmnl.com as your information server with a 14-day free trial. After that, you’ll need to pay a one-time $50 license fee to keep your device connected to TRMNL servers.

If you’d rather go your own way, Seeed offers software options, including Home Assistant compatibility, that don’t require a TRMNL connection or license. You can also access the SenseCraft Seeedash platform, which includes a plugin repository and design workspace. It’s worth checking out the options before committing to a $50 TRMNL license. The browser-based platform also includes a firmware-flashing tool Seeed describes as simple enough for anyone to use.

If you already have a server up and running, you can point the device right at it. Terminus is TRMNL’s open source container for this setup. The Terminus GitHub page describes the BYOS as providing “privacy first functionality by empowering you to run your own private server, network, and devices. You own the stack and the data.”

The e-paper display and control board simply ping an API to retrieve the information to display. You can even write plugins in HTML, which the screen renders as a bitmap. The trade-off is that your server needs to stay online, and maintaining it may bring some system-admin headaches some users may want to avoid. But hey, that’s why there are options.

An example of a weather app on the Seeed firmware.

What’s in the box?

  • XIAO ePaper Display Dev Board with XIAO ESP32-S3 Plus onboard
  • 7.5-inch monochrome ePaper display (800 × 480 pixels)
  • FPC extension cable (10 cm)
  • FPC connector
  • 2,000 mAh rechargeable Li-ion battery
  • Wi-Fi antenna

Two official case designs are available for 3D printing: a triangular prism and an L-shaped case. I went for the latter, and although I’d hoped assembly would be as simple as plugging everything in and slotting the pieces into place, it proved to be a bit more involved.

The kit came with all the hardware I needed, with one slight hiccup: I’d forgotten to order a case or display stand. Fortunately, TRMNL is a proper DIY project, and there are print files available for recommended stand setups. A quick print at my local library’s Bambu printer and $8 solved the problem. I probably should have chosen something other than “dealer’s choice” for the PLA color, as I ended up with a bright canary yellow device case. At least it stands out on my kitchen countertop.

I’d recommend trying the prism shell design over the L-style case I chose because the latter required me to cut a channel for the ribbon cable extension. It wasn’t a huge deal for a project like this, but you may need to do some extra work and fiddle with the fit. You’ll also need needle-nose pliers to remove the print’s support trees from the narrow space.

Assembly

Before trying to fit everything into the printed case, I wanted to make sure the hardware worked, so I connected the parts on my workbench. The case-less assembly couldn’t be simpler: Connect the battery or a USB-C power source, plug the display directly into the board, and you’re good to go. From there, connect your phone or tablet to the device’s Wi-Fi and enter your local Wi-Fi credentials.

If you attempt this build, be aware that it involves some delicate parts. The FPC is extremely fragile and can break if you force it to bend in a direction it doesn’t want to go (say, around the sharp angle of an L-shaped case). Getting the cable to conform to the design was challenging; I tried using tweezers to coax the cable around the bend but got nowhere fast.

Connecting and routing the ribbon cable extension was the most stressful part of the assembly. The case design just doesn’t accommodate the path the ribbon cable naturally wants to take. Following a helpful tip from a commenter on MakerWorld, I managed to snake the cable through the narrow passage by attaching a bit of paper tape to the end of the ribbon connector.

After powering on the kit for the first time, you’ll see the TRMNL logo and a QR code on the e-paper display. Scanning the code redirects you to a “How to set up a new device” guide written by Kulp, the TRMNL creator. The guide had been updated just 15 minutes before I clicked the link—a promising sign of a living document that is constantly evolving.

TRMNL.com

I wasn’t planning to use the trmnl.com service, but I wanted to get a sense of what it offered for its $50 access fee. The 14-day “free” trial is a misnomer, though. Before you can register your device, you’ll need to enter your credit card information and pay $1 for access. After plopping down a buck, the next screen welcomed me to my trial.

After registering your kit’s MAC address with trmnl.com, you’ll receive what the service calls a “friendly code,” a much shorter identifier that’s easier to remember than an entire MAC address. From there, you can install plugins to display content on a schedule throughout the day.

The options are vast. The marketplace contains standard fare like Google Calendar, weather, and stock quotes, alongside more niche offerings like rotating factoids about the Ferengi Rules of Acquisition in Star Trek.

If you’re looking for a hassle-free solution that “just works,” it’s hard to fault the package trmnl.com has put together. I’m a fan of any service that offers a one-time license fee over yet another forever subscription, and I think $50 is a fair price for the people behind the platform to be compensated for their work. After all, it handles all the rendering; the device simply displays information pulled from the APIs.

SenseCraft

On the Seeed side, there’s SenseCraft, a similar marketplace to trmnl.com’s but without the license fee. The website offers a browser-based flashing tool that promises to “flash official firmware from the browser. No coding. No terminal. Just clicks.”

The process was as simple as promised—once I figured out that I needed a USB-C to USB-C cable. I connected the board to my PC via the onboard USB-C port, opened the website in a Chromium-based browser (sorry, Firefox), selected my device from a drop-down menu, and clicked “Flash.” Once the device rebooted, setup followed essentially the same process as it did with TRMNL, minus the credit card. The tradeoff for free access is that Seeed is based in China and operates under its own privacy policy. Your call, but it’s certainly nice to have options.

After registering a Seeed account, I entered a code displayed on the device, just as I had with TRMNL. SenseCraft’s marketplace is similarly packed with community contributions, but I had trouble determining which plugins were intended for my device and which might not be compatible. I tried publishing several different feeds to the display, but I couldn’t get them to render.

SenseCraft leans heavily into AI-powered custom designs. While the platform offers a bit of everything, much of its content is geared toward the Chinese market, with English-language apps sprinkled throughout. I can see why US users reached out to ask about TRMNL compatibility.

Bring your own server

As TRMNL puts it, “the goal isn’t for BYOS to match parity with our hosted solution but to provide enough of a pleasant solution for your own customized experience.” Even a modest homelab server should have no trouble running the Terminus package, which acts as an API point that takes in information, renders the designs, and sends them to your e-paper display. The process shouldn’t put meaningful strain on most systems.

It’s great that there’s an “easy” version for a fee, but homelabbing is one of my favorite hobbies, and I love self-hosting projects wherever possible. When I first saw the DIY TRMNL/Seeed package, I was hoping I’d be able to control the feed myself.

For now, getting Terminus running on your server isn’t as simple as heading to your OS’s Docker app store and downloading a host service. TRMNL has a great guide to walk you through the setup, but if you’re not comfortable working with docker compose files, you may want to pay the one-time license fee and leave the hosting to TRMNL.

I won’t lie: I spent some late nights banging my head against the desk trying to get everything running. I’d initially tried hosting it on my main Unraid machine, but I kept running into bridge networking issues. The Terminus package is a multi-container compose stack with pieces like Sidekiq worker, Postgres, Valkey, and a certificate initializer. If those containers can’t communicate with each other, nothing works.

Thankfully, I’m a weird nerd who also runs a CasaOS deployment on another machine. After I executed the bin/setup script there, everything worked as it should. The next issue was flashing back to the latest TRMNL firmware package. My unit arrived with FW 1.5.12, well behind the current 1.8.18 release.

Flashing proved to be an annoyance again because I struggled to keep the unit in flashing mode and get the web flasher to communicate with the serial port on my Fedora PC. After about 30 minutes of troubleshooting without making progress, I switched to my MacBook Pro, where the process worked on the first try. Go figure.

Once you’ve updated the display to the proper firmware and pointed its connections at your server, you can write and design your own display templates. If starting from scratch isn’t your thing, TRMNL’s own plugins repo and a community-maintained catalog are available. A new Extensions Gallery in the Terminus web UI lets you import certain plugins for local hosting.

The options are almost overwhelming, and I imagine it will take some time to get everything dialed in exactly as I want it. I still plan to stick with the BYOS route, but the process isn’t as straightforward as I had hoped. For example, the setting for pointing the display at your local server is hidden under the “advanced” settings page during the web portal login.

Real-world impressions

Once I deployed the display in my kitchen, I could get a better sense of how it would fit into my day-to-day life. The 7.5-inch e-paper display is large enough to read from across the room, and all the plugins I had running looked crisp and legible. My son was enamored with the lunar cycles display and commented that “now I’ll always know what moon we have.”

That’s where the kit shines: showing little rotating bursts of useful information that you might never have thought to look up before.

Seeed Studio says the display can run for three months on battery power. I haven’t had the device long enough to verify that claim, but I’m not sure I need the battery for much more than backup. The device powers via USB just fine, so I’ll probably leave it connected to a nearby hub on the counter. The three-month estimate assumes that the display will update once every six hours. I prefer refreshes closer to once an hour, which would cut battery life significantly. Either way, the battery becomes largely irrelevant if you use a USB power source.

Final thoughts

The official TRMNL route is starting to look mighty tempting if it means getting the type of headache-free, set-it-and-forget-it Ron Popeil experience I was expecting from this setup. I’ll keep tinkering with the BYOS solutions, but since those still run on the official TRMNL firmware, I may switch back and use the rest of my 14-day trial to see what best suits my needs. The $50 license fee would push my total project cost over $100. That’s not a huge deal, but it’s double what I was expecting.

The TRMNL/Seeed Studio collaboration has produced a true DIY device. It will never compete with a home assistant device from Amazon or Apple, but it’s not meant to, and that’s a good thing. Not everyone wants a digital butler waiting for their next command. Sometimes you just want information that’s relevant to you and your life, displayed in a central place in your home.
